claim: TRPV3 is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes.
source: The multimodal sensory channel transient receptor potential vanilloid-3 (TRPV3) is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and implicated in chronic pruritus, allergy, and inflammation-related skin disorders.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Chung et al., 2004b; Peier et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2002).

claim: TRPV3 is implicated in chronic pruritus, allergy, and inflammation-related skin disorders.
source: The multimodal sensory channel transient receptor potential vanilloid-3 (TRPV3) is expressed in epidermal keratinocytes and implicated in chronic pruritus, allergy, and inflammation-related skin disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references throughout the manuscript.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations of TRPV3 cause hair growth disorders in mice.
source: Gain-of-function mutations of TRPV3 cause hair growth disorders in mice and Olmsted syndrome in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Asakawa et al., 2006).

claim: Gain-of-function mutations of TRPV3 cause Olmsted syndrome in humans.
source: Gain-of-function mutations of TRPV3 cause hair growth disorders in mice and Olmsted syndrome in humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Agarwala et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2012).

claim: Dyclonine inhibits mouse TRPV3 channel.
source: We here report that mouse and human TRPV3 channel is targeted by the clinical medication dyclonine that exerts a potent inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings showing dose-dependent inhibition (Figure 1).

claim: Dyclonine inhibits human TRPV3 channel.
source: We here report that mouse and human TRPV3 channel is targeted by the clinical medication dyclonine that exerts a potent inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings (Figure 2D-F).

claim: Dyclonine rescued cell death caused by gain-of-function TRPV3 mutations.
source: Accordingly, dyclonine rescued cell death caused by gain-of-function TRPV3 mutations and suppressed pruritus symptoms in vivo in mouse model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry analysis and microscopy (Figure 5).

claim: Dyclonine suppressed pruritus symptoms in vivo in mouse model.
source: Accordingly, dyclonine rescued cell death caused by gain-of-function TRPV3 mutations and suppressed pruritus symptoms in vivo in mouse model.
evidence: This is demonstrated through scratching behavior experiments (Figure 6).

claim: Dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 open probability at the single-channel level.
source: At the single-channel level, dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 open probability but not the unitary conductance.
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-channel recordings (Figure 7).

claim: Dyclonine does not affect TRPV3 unitary conductance.
source: At the single-channel level, dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 open probability but not the unitary conductance.
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-channel recordings showing no change in conductance (Figure 7C).

claim: Key residues in TRPV3 pore region toggle the inhibitory efficiency of dyclonine.
source: By molecular simulations and mutagenesis, we further uncovered key residues in TRPV3 pore region that could toggle the inhibitory efficiency of dyclonine.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis experiments (Figure 8).

claim: TRPV3 channels belong to a family of calcium-permeable and nonselective cation channels.
source: Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels belong to a family of calcium-permeable and nonselective cation channels, essential for body sensory processing and local inflammatory development (Clapham, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: TRPV3 is abundantly expressed in skin keratinocytes.
source: As a polymodal cellular sensor, transient receptor potential vanilloid-3 (TRPV3) channel is abundantly expressed in skin keratinocytes (Chung et al., 2004b; Peier et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2002) and in cells surrounding the hair follicles (Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: TRPV3 is expressed in cells surrounding the hair follicles.
source: As a polymodal cellular sensor, transient receptor potential vanilloid-3 (TRPV3) channel is abundantly expressed in skin keratinocytes (Chung et al., 2004b; Peier et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2002) and in cells surrounding the hair follicles (Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: TRPV3 is sensitive to innocuous temperatures above 30–33°C.
source: TRPV3 is sensitive to innocuous temperatures above 30–33°C and exhibits an increased response at noxious temperature (Chung et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Camphor activates TRPV3.
source: Natural plant products such as camphor (Moqrich et al., 2005), carvacrol, eugenol, thymol (Xu et al., 2006), and the pharmacological compound 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB) (Chung et al., 2004a; Colton and Zhu, 2007) also activate TRPV3.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: 2-APB activates TRPV3.
source: Natural plant products such as camphor (Moqrich et al., 2005), carvacrol, eugenol, thymol (Xu et al., 2006), and the pharmacological compound 2-aminoethoxydiphenyl borate (2-APB) (Chung et al., 2004a; Colton and Zhu, 2007) also activate TRPV3.
evidence: This is stated with citation support and used throughout the experiments.

claim: TRPV3 is directly activated by acidic pH from cytoplasmic side.
source: In addition, TRPV3 is directly activated by acidic pH from cytoplasmic side (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The Gly573Ser substitution in TRPV3 renders the channel spontaneously active.
source: In rodents, the Gly573Ser substitution in TRPV3 renders the channel spontaneously active and caused a hairless phenotype in DS-Nh mice and WBN/Kob-Ht rats (Asakawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The Gly573Ser substitution in TRPV3 caused a hairless phenotype in DS-Nh mice.
source: In rodents, the Gly573Ser substitution in TRPV3 renders the channel spontaneously active and caused a hairless phenotype in DS-Nh mice and WBN/Kob-Ht rats (Asakawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: DS-Nh mice develop severe scratching behavior and pruritic dermatitis.
source: DS-Nh mice also develop severe scratching behavior and pruritic dermatitis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: TRPV3-deficient mice give rise to phenotypes of curly whiskers and wavy hair coat.
source: Furthermore, TRPV3-deficient mice give rise to phenotypes of curly whiskers and wavy hair coat (Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Dyclonine is a clinical anesthetic characterized by rapid onset of effect, lack of systemic toxicity, and low index of sensitization.
source: Dyclonine is a clinical anesthetic characterized by rapid onset of effect, lack of systemic toxicity, and low index of sensitization (Florestano and Bahler, 1956).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Topical application of dyclonine rapidly relieves itching and pain in patients.
source: Its topical application (0.5% or 1% dyclonine hydrochloride contained in the topical solution, i.e., ~30.7 mM at a dose of 1%, according to the United States Pharmacopeia) rapidly relieves itching and pain in patients by ameliorating inflamed, excoriated, and broken lesions on mucous membranes and skin (Morginson et al., 1956).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Dyclonine is used to anesthetize mucous membranes prior to endoscopy.
source: Accordingly, dyclonine is used to anesthetize mucous membranes prior to endoscopy (Formaker et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: 5 μM dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 currents to 30% ± 2% of control level.
source: The presence of 5 and 10 µM dyclonine significantly inhibited TRPV3 currents response to 30% ± 2% and 15% ± 3% of control level, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings (Figure 1A,B).

claim: 10 μM dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 currents to 15% ± 3% of control level.
source: The presence of 5 and 10 µM dyclonine significantly inhibited TRPV3 currents response to 30% ± 2% and 15% ± 3% of control level, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings (Figure 1A,B).

claim: The blocking effect of dyclonine on TRPV3 is reversible.
source: After washing out of dyclonine, 2-APB evoked a similar response to the control level, indicating that the blocking effect of dyclonine is reversible (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings showing recovery after washout.

claim: Dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 currents in a concentration-dependent manner with an IC50 of 3.2 ± 0.24 μM.
source: The dose-response curve indicates that dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 currents in a concentration-dependent manner with an IC50 of 3.2 ± 0.24 μM (n = 6, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments (Figure 1C).

claim: TRPV3 channels exhibit sensitizing properties upon repeated stimulation.
source: Because TRPV3 channels exhibit sensitizing properties upon repeated stimulation (Chung et al., 2004a), we examined the effect of dyclonine after the response had stabilized following repetitive application of 2-APB (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and demonstrated in experiments.

claim: The presence of dyclonine significantly slowed down the TRPV3 sensitization process.
source: The presence of dyclonine significantly slowed down this process, requiring ~16 repetitions to reach the current level of full sensitization (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through repeated stimulation experiments (Figure 1G-I).

claim: Dyclonine effectively suppresses the activity of endogenous TRPV3 channels in mouse keratinocytes.
source: Thus, dyclonine effectively suppresses the activity of endogenous TRPV3 channels in mouse keratinocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments in primary mouse keratinocytes (Figure 1J-L).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine for inhibiting TRPV3 in keratinocytes was 5.2 ± 0.71 μM.
source: From the dose-response curve (Figure 1L), the IC50 of dyclonine was assessed to be 5.2 ± 0.71 μM, with a Hill coefficient of nH = 2.4 ± 0.75 (n = 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments in keratinocytes (Figure 1L).

claim: 10 μM dyclonine exhibited little inhibition on TRPV1, TRPV2, TRPM8, and TRPA1.
source: We observed that 10 μM dyclonine exhibited little inhibition on TRPV1, TRPV2, TRPM8, and TRPA1, but potently inhibited TRPV3 channel (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative experiments (Figure 2A,B).

claim: 10 μM dyclonine caused 87% ± 1% inhibition of TRPV3 current.
source: The corresponding reduction in current amplitude was 2% ± 1% for TRPV1, 6% ± 1% for TRPV2, 9% ± 2% for TRPM8, 5% ± 1% for TRPA1, compared with 87% ± 1% inhibition of TRPV3 current (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative experiments (Figure 2B).

claim: Dyclonine represents an effective inhibitor of TRPV3 channel.
source: The corresponding IC50 values of dyclonine for inhibiting TRPV1, TRPV2, TRPM8, and TRPA1 channels (336.3 ± 12.0 μM, 36.5 ± 3.7 μM, 72.4 ± 10.9 μM, and 152.35 ± 16.3 μM, respectively) were one or two orders of magnitude higher than that for TRPV3 inhibition (3.2 ± 0.24 μM), indicating that dyclonine represents an effective inhibitor of TRPV3 channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative IC50 values (Figure 2C).

claim: The inhibition of TRPV3 by dyclonine is conserved across species.
source: Therefore, the inhibition of TRPV3 by dyclonine is conserved across species.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with mouse, human, and frog TRPV3 (Figure 2D-I).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine for human TRPV3 was 16.2 ± 0.72 μM.
source: Dose-response curves for dyclonine inhibition yielded an IC50 value of 16.2 ± 0.72 μM for hTRPV3 and 12.3 ± 1.6 μM for fTRPV3, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments (Figure 2F).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine for frog TRPV3 was 12.3 ± 1.6 μM.
source: Dose-response curves for dyclonine inhibition yielded an IC50 value of 16.2 ± 0.72 μM for hTRPV3 and 12.3 ± 1.6 μM for fTRPV3, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments (Figure 2I).

claim: Dyclonine inhibits TRPV3 in a voltage-independent manner.
source: We found no significant difference inhibition at hyperpolarized voltages versus depolarized voltages, showing that the inhibition occurred independently of the membrane potential (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through voltage-step experiments (Figure 3).

claim: Ruthenium red only inhibited TRPV3 channel currents at negative potentials while enhanced TRPV3 currents at positive potentials.
source: Note that dyclonine had an inhibitory effect on TRPV3 currents at both positive and negative potentials, but RR only inhibited TRPV3 channel currents at negative potentials while enhanced TRPV3 currents at positive potentials (blue trace).
evidence: This is demonstrated through voltage-step experiments (Figure 3B).

claim: TRPV3 is a thermal-sensitive ion channel with an activation threshold around 30–33°C.
source: TRPV3 is a thermal-sensitive ion channel and has an activation threshold around 30–33°C (Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Dyclonine dose-dependently suppresses heat-evoked TRPV3 currents.
source: These results thus indicate that dyclonine dose-dependently suppresses heat-evoked TRPV3 currents.
evidence: This is demonstrated through temperature-jump experiments (Figure 4).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine on heat-activated TRPV3 inhibition was 14.02 ± 2.5 μM.
source: The IC50 of dyclonine on TRPV3 inhibition was assessed to be 14.02 ± 2.5 μM with a Hill coefficient of nH = 1.9 ± 0.54, according to the dose-response curve fitting (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments with heat activation (Figure 4E).

claim: Gain-of-function mutations G573S and G573C of TRPV3 are constitutively active.
source: It has previously been reported that gain-of-function mutations, G573S and G573C, of TRPV3 are constitutively active and their expression causes cell death (Xiao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Expression of G573S and G573C TRPV3 mutants causes cell death.
source: It has previously been reported that gain-of-function mutations, G573S and G573C, of TRPV3 are constitutively active and their expression causes cell death (Xiao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support and demonstrated in experiments (Figure 5).

claim: 10 μM dyclonine reduced spontaneous activities from G573S by 74% ± 3%.
source: By subtracting leak currents, we found that spontaneous activities from G573S and G573C were reduced by 74% ± 3% (n = 6) and 71% ± 2% (n = 6) by 10 μM dyclonine, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings (Figure 5A-C).

claim: 10 μM dyclonine reduced spontaneous activities from G573C by 71% ± 2%.
source: By subtracting leak currents, we found that spontaneous activities from G573S and G573C were reduced by 74% ± 3% (n = 6) and 71% ± 2% (n = 6) by 10 μM dyclonine, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings (Figure 5A-C).

claim: Dyclonine largely prevented cell death caused by G573C and G573S TRPV3 mutants.
source: Addition of dyclonine largely prevented the cell death while not causing change in the expression of TRPV3 channels (Figure 5E), indicating that dyclonine decreased the cytotoxicity caused by the gain-of-function mutants.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy and flow cytometry (Figure 5E-G).

claim: Dyclonine rescues cell death by inhibiting the excessive activity of TRPV3 channel.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that dyclonine rescues cell death by inhibiting the excessive activity of TRPV3 channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell death assays (Figure 5).

claim: Intradermal injection of carvacrol in WT TRPV3 mice caused significant increases in scratching bouts.
source: Intradermal injection of carvacrol (0.1%, 50 μl) in WT TRPV3 mice caused significant increases in the accumulated scratching bouts (137.2 ± 33.9) compared to the control group receiving normal saline (0.9% NaCl, 3.8 ± 1, n = 6, p<0.001; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral experiments (Figure 6A,B).

claim: Intradermal injection of carvacrol did not elicit a remarkable change in scratching bouts in TRPV3-/- mice.
source: By contrast, intradermal injection of carvacrol (0.1%, 50 μl) did not elicit a remarkable change in the number of scratching bouts in TRPV3-/- mice (Figure 6A,B), supporting that carvacrol caused itching-scratching behavior via TRPV3 activation (Cui et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral experiments in knockout mice (Figure 6A,B).

claim: Dyclonine ameliorates TRPV3 hyperactivity-caused scratching in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Hence, dyclonine ameliorates TRPV3 hyperactivity-caused scratching in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral experiments with different dyclonine concentrations (Figure 6C,D).

claim: Dyclonine inhibited carvacrol-activated TRPV3 currents in a concentration-dependent manner with IC50 = 3.5 ± 0.34 μM.
source: Similar to that observed with the inhibition of 2-APB-evoked TRPV3 currents (Figure 1A–C), dyclonine also inhibited carvacrol-activated TRPV3 currents in a concentration-dependent manner with IC50 = 3.5 ± 0.34 μM following sensitization by repeated application of 300 μM 2-APB (n = 8, Figure 6E,F), implying that the itching caused by carvacrol is mainly due to the activation of TRPV3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole-cell recordings (Figure 6E,F).

claim: Dyclonine showed little effect on electrophysiological responses in mouse DRG and TG neurons.
source: In contrast, dyclonine (10 μM) showed little effect on electrophysiological responses in mouse dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and trigeminal ganglia (TG) neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through current-clamp recordings (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: The in vivo effect of dyclonine arises from the targeting of keratinocyte TRPV3 channels.
source: This observation is in line with the absence of TRPV3 in mouse DRGs (Peier et al., 2002) and suggests that the invio effect of dyclonine arises from the targeting of keratinocyte TRPV3 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect on DRG/TG neurons and the known expression pattern of TRPV3.

claim: Dyclonine decreased the single-channel open probability from 0.8 ± 0.02 to 0.08 ± 0.01 at –60 mV.
source: We observed that the single-channel open probability was largely decreased by dyclonine from 0.8 ± 0.02 to 0.08 ± 0.01 at –60 mV and from 0.82 ± 0.02 to 0.12 ± 0.01 at +60 mV (n = 6), respectively (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-channel recordings (Figure 7A,B).

claim: Dyclonine decreased the single-channel open probability from 0.82 ± 0.02 to 0.12 ± 0.01 at +60 mV.
source: We observed that the single-channel open probability was largely decreased by dyclonine from 0.8 ± 0.02 to 0.08 ± 0.01 at –60 mV and from 0.82 ± 0.02 to 0.12 ± 0.01 at +60 mV (n = 6), respectively (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-channel recordings (Figure 7A,B).

claim: Dyclonine had no effect on single TRPV3 channel conductance.
source: Statistical analysis, however, revealed that dyclonine had no effect on single TRPV3 channel conductance (163.6 ± 6.4 pS vs. 179.2 ± 5.5 pS for before and after dyclonine treatment; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-channel I-V analysis (Figure 7C).

claim: Dyclonine is not a competitive antagonist of TRPV3.
source: Dyclonine inhibited TRPV3 currents evoked by both 2-APB (Figure 1) and heat (Figure 4), implying that dyclonine is not a competitive antagonist.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that dyclonine inhibits TRPV3 activated by different stimuli.

claim: Dyclonine is not simply an open channel blocker.
source: In addition, the voltage independence of dyclonine inhibition and the fact that dyclonine is a positive charged alkaloid suggest that dyclonine is not simply an open channel blocker.
evidence: This is inferred from the voltage-independence data and chemical properties of dyclonine.

claim: Mutations L630W, N643A, I644W, and L655A greatly reduced the inhibitory effect of dyclonine.
source: Among the mutants, mutations L630W, N643A, I644W, and L655A greatly reduced the inhibitory effect of dyclonine, whereas the mutants L642A and I659A showed higher sensitivity to dyclonine than WT channel (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis experiments (Figure 8C-E).

claim: Mutants L642A and I659A showed higher sensitivity to dyclonine than WT channel.
source: Among the mutants, mutations L630W, N643A, I644W, and L655A greatly reduced the inhibitory effect of dyclonine, whereas the mutants L642A and I659A showed higher sensitivity to dyclonine than WT channel (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mutagenesis experiments (Figure 8C-E).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine for L655A mutant was 286.7 ± 10.4 μM.
source: The dose-response curves were fitted with a Hill equation, and the corresponding IC50 values for each TRPV3 mutant were as follows: IC50 = 286.7 ± 10.4 μM for L655A; IC50 = 30.8 ± 2.2 μM for L630W; IC50 = 37.7 ± 5.1 μM for N643A; IC50 = 26.1 ± 2.8 μM for I644W; IC50 = 0.25 ± 0.02 μM for L642A; and IC50 = 0.56 ± 0.06 μM for I659A compared to IC50 = 3.2 ± 0.24 μM for WT TRPV3 (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments (Figure 8D,E).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine for L642A mutant was 0.25 ± 0.02 μM.
source: The dose-response curves were fitted with a Hill equation, and the corresponding IC50 values for each TRPV3 mutant were as follows: IC50 = 286.7 ± 10.4 μM for L655A; IC50 = 30.8 ± 2.2 μM for L630W; IC50 = 37.7 ± 5.1 μM for N643A; IC50 = 26.1 ± 2.8 μM for I644W; IC50 = 0.25 ± 0.02 μM for L642A; and IC50 = 0.56 ± 0.06 μM for I659A compared to IC50 = 3.2 ± 0.24 μM for WT TRPV3 (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments (Figure 8D,E).

claim: The IC50 of dyclonine for I659A mutant was 0.56 ± 0.06 μM.
source: The dose-response curves were fitted with a Hill equation, and the corresponding IC50 values for each TRPV3 mutant were as follows: IC50 = 286.7 ± 10.4 μM for L655A; IC50 = 30.8 ± 2.2 μM for L630W; IC50 = 37.7 ± 5.1 μM for N643A; IC50 = 26.1 ± 2.8 μM for I644W; IC50 = 0.25 ± 0.02 μM for L642A; and IC50 = 0.56 ± 0.06 μM for I659A compared to IC50 = 3.2 ± 0.24 μM for WT TRPV3 (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through dose-response experiments (Figure 8D,E).

claim: MTSET modification caused reduced dyclonine blockade in L630C, F633C, and L642C but not WT TRPV3.
source: Along the same line, MTSET modification caused reduced dyclonine blockade in L630C, F633C, and L642C but not WT TRPV3, and DTT restored the blockage of dyclonine in these mutants (Figure 8I), implying that dyclonine-mediated inhibition is mediated by the region predicted by BMA binding mode.
evidence: This is demonstrated through chemical modification experiments (Figure 8G-I).

claim: Dyclonine interacts with the pore cavity of TRPV3 likely behaving as a negative allosteric modulator.
source: Together, our results suggest that dyclonine interacts with the pore cavity of TRPV3 likely behaving as a negative allosteric modulator.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis and docking studies (Figure 8).

claim: Dyclonine has been used for clinical treatment of itching and pain for decades.
source: Dyclonine is a topical antipruritic agent and has been used for clinical treatment of itching and pain for decades (Gargiulo et al., 1992; Greifenstein et al., 1956).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Dyclonine is a condition-across inhibitor of TRPV3.
source: Such inhibition was observed for TRPV3 responses to both chemical and thermal activation, suggesting that dyclonine is a condition-across inhibitor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dyclonine inhibits TRPV3 activated by different stimuli.

claim: Dyclonine may be used to alleviate skin inflammations persisted in physiological temperatures.
source: As TRPV3 responds to moderate temperatures (30–40°C), dyclonine may thus be used to alleviate skin inflammations persisted in physiological temperatures.
evidence: This is speculated based on the temperature sensitivity of TRPV3 and dyclonine's inhibitory effect.

claim: Dyclonine has shown its safety to human body.
source: Also, as a clinical drug dyclonine has been widely used and thus has shown its safety to human body (Gargiulo et al., 1992; Sahdeo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Dyclonine can be a research tool to dissect the physiological and pathological characteristics of TRPV3 channel.
source: In addition, as a potent inhibitor, dyclonine can also been a research tool to dissect the physiological and pathological characteristics of TRPV3 channel.
evidence: This is suggested based on the potent and specific inhibition of TRPV3 by dyclonine.

claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels have been shown to be inhibited by local anesthetics including dyclonine.
source: For instance, voltage-gated sodium channels have been shown to be inhibited by local anesthetics including dyclonine (Sahdeo et al., 2014; Tikhonov and Zhorov, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Binding of dyclonine into the BMA pocket could prevent the structural rearrangements of pore loop during TRPV3 gating.
source: Likely, binding of dyclonine into this pocket could prevent the structural rearrangements of pore loop during TRPV3 gating, implying that dyclonine behaves as a negative allosteric modulator.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and mutagenesis data.

claim: The amino acids that make up the pocket and the precise shape of the pocket are diverse among TRP channels.
source: Although similar pockets can also be observed on other TRP channels, the amino acids that make up the pocket and the precise shape of the pocket are diverse (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sequence alignment (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

claim: The diversity in pocket composition may explain why TRPV3 is specifically targeted by dyclonine.
source: This may be the reason why TRPV3 is targeted by dyclonine (Liao et al., 2013; Shimada et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences between TRP channels.
